screens.title: SNMP: Purpose and MIBs
screens.narratorSegment: Simple Network Management Protocol, or SNMP, is the foundational protocol for device telemetry. At its core, SNMP lets an external manager query device variables or receive asynchronous notifications called traps or informs. These variables are defined in a Management Information Base, a hierarchical database of objects such as interface counters, C P U utilization, and memory usage. The MIB gives each variable a structured identifier so monitoring systems can consistently collect the same metrics from different vendors. A concrete example: an NMS polling ifInOctets and ifOutOctets from the interface table to compute link utilization over time. A common misconception is that SNMP alone explains traffic patterns. It does not: SNMP tells you counters and state, but not which flows caused the traffic. That’s where NetFlow comes in. When you configure SNMP, you must choose access controls and a version. SNMPv1 and v2c use community strings that are sent in clear text and therefore should be limited to trusted networks and read-only when possible. SNMPv3 provides authentication and encryption and is required for production. Key takeaway: use SNMP to collect device health and state, rely on MIB structure to map metrics across devices, and prefer SNMPv3 to secure that telemetry. How will you map MIB variables to the metrics you care about in your environment?

screens.title: Configuring SNMP on Cisco Devices
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring SNMP involves enabling the protocol, defining who may read or write variables, and restricting which systems can query or receive traps. For SNMPv2c a common minimal setup is a read-only community string and a host that will receive traps. A common example in a lab is creating a read-only community and pointing traps to the monitoring server, then enabling traps on the device. For production it's better to use SNMPv3: you create a view to control which OIDs are visible, a group with security parameters, and a user bound to that group with authentication and privacy. The concrete verification steps are important: after configuration, run show snmp to confirm communities or users, and check the NMS for trap delivery. A frequent misconception is that enabling SNMP alone secures monitoring; it does not — you must restrict access with ACLs and prefer SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption. In the lab you'll paste the example commands into a simulated router, then use show commands to verify each step. Reflect: what ACLs will you create to limit SNMP access to your NMS?

Commands (examples)
Paste these into a simulated router to create a read-only v2c community and a simple SNMPv3 user.
Router(config)# snmp-server community cohortia_ro RO
Router(config)# snmp-server host 192.168.1.100 traps version 2c cohortia_ro
Router(config)# snmp-server enable traps

! SNMPv3 minimal example
Router(config)# snmp-server view V1 iso included
Router(config)# snmp-server group GROUP1 v3 priv read V1 write V1
Router(config)# snmp-server user USER1 GROUP1 v3 auth sha AUTH_PASS priv aes 256 PRIV_PASS
Router(config)# snmp-server host 192.168.1.100 informs version 3 USER1

  • Run show snmp to confirm communities and users are present.
  • Check the NMS for trap/inform arrival after generating an event.
  • Verify ACLs allow NMS IPs to query SNMP ports.

Not restricting snmp-server host or forgetting to enable traps leads to missed notifications or open access.

screens.title: NetFlow & IPFIX: Flow-Level Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: NetFlow and IPFIX capture metadata about network flows — records that describe source and destination IPs, ports, protocols, and byte and packet counts. Unlike SNMP, which reports counters and state, flow telemetry shows who communicated with whom, which protocols were used, and which conversation carried the most bytes. A practical example: when a core router's C P U spikes, NetFlow on that router helps you identify a top talker or a heavy protocol that coincides with the spike. NetFlow collectors aggregate these records and present top talkers, protocol distributions, and time-series trends useful for capacity planning and anomaly detection. Common misconceptions include believing NetFlow outputs full packet contents; it does not carry payloads, only metadata. Also, enabling NetFlow indiscriminately on all interfaces or without sampling can overload a router's C P U and the collector. Planning which interfaces to monitor and choosing sensible timeouts and sampling rates helps balance visibility and device load. Key takeaway: use NetFlow/IPFIX for traffic forensic capability and capacity insight, but plan your exporter, monitoring interfaces, and sampling strategy carefully to avoid performance problems. In practical terms, what flow records contain and why they matter for capacity and security. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Router(config)# ip flow-export version 9

A concrete example: configure logging host 192.168.1.100 and set logging trap informational to send messages at informational severity and above. A common mistake is forwarding debug-level messages in production — this can flood log storage and hide critical alerts. Key takeaway: centralize logs, pick balanced trap levels, and use facilities to categorize messages for easier analysis and retention policies. What logging level matches your organization's incident response goals? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a practical mental model for network monitoring and why it matters. Monitoring is not passive logging; it is continuous visibility that turns raw device signals into actionable insight. We will use four complementary tools: SNMP for device health and event notifications, NetFlow or IPFIX for flow-level traffic patterns, Syslog for centralized event capture and correlation, and IP SLA for synthetic, active performance checks. Together these tools let you establish a baseline — a snapshot of normal behavior — and then configure alerts when important metrics deviate. For example, collecting interface utilization via SNMP and flow metadata via NetFlow lets you differentiate a C P U spike caused by a traffic surge from a misconfiguration or a software bug. Throughout the chapter you will see configuration examples you can paste into a simulated router, learn common mistakes like using weak SNMP community strings or sending debug-level syslog to production, and practice a hands-on scenario that ties SNMP, NetFlow, Syslog, and IP SLA to a single monitoring server. By the end you will know how to collect the right signals, create a baseline, and configure alerts that reduce noisy alarms while catching real incidents early. What problem will you solve first with this visibility?

These objectives focus your work on measurable monitoring skills you can use in the lab and on real networks. First, you'll configure and verify SNMP so devices expose useful telemetry and send traps when events occur. That includes choosing a secure SNMP version, setting community strings or users, and restricting access. Second, you will implement NetFlow or IPFIX to collect flow metadata for capacity planning and anomaly detection, learning exporter and monitor setup and the practical tradeoffs of sampling and interface selection. Third, you'll configure Syslog to centralize event logging and choose an appropriate severity level so critical messages are visible without overwhelming the server. Finally, you'll start working with IP SLA to create active checks for latency, jitter, and packet loss to critical endpoints. Each objective is paired with verification steps so you can confirm your configuration in the simulator. These skills matter because they let you move from reactive firefighting to proactive detection and faster root-cause identification. These additional objectives focus on applied skills that make monitoring actionable. First, you will develop baselining strategies: collecting SNMP counters, NetFlow summaries, and IP SLA results over time to define normal ranges. This matters because an alert without context is noise; baselines help you tune thresholds. Second, you will practice hands-on verification: running show commands to confirm SNMP traps, NetFlow exporters, syslog reachability, and IP SLA statistics. The lab workflow shows specific verification commands so you can confirm behavior in a simulator. Third, you will apply security and access controls for monitoring protocols — restricting SNMP access with ACLs, preferring SNMPv3, and avoiding default community strings. Finally, you will analyze how to use flow data for incident response and capacity planning, recognizing when NetFlow points you to a top talker versus when the issue is C P U or misconfiguration. Each card also includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the verification step. These skills turn telemetry into reliable, low-noise alerts that guide remediation.

Simple Network Management Protocol, or SNMP, is the foundational protocol for device telemetry. At its core, SNMP lets an external manager query device variables or receive asynchronous notifications called traps or informs. NetFlow and IPFIX capture metadata about network flows — records that describe source and destination IPs, ports, protocols, and byte and packet counts. Unlike SNMP, which reports counters and state, flow telemetry shows who communicated with whom, which protocols were used, and which conversation carried the most bytes. A practical example: when a core router's C P U spikes, NetFlow on that router helps you identify a top talker or a heavy protocol that coincides with the spike. NetFlow collectors aggregate these records and present top talkers, protocol distributions, and time-series trends useful for capacity planning and anomaly detection.
